extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying and characterizing causes, laws, and lawful uniformities in scientific explanation—distinguishing unconditional causes from mere invariable sequences, understanding dispositions/properties as conditions, and separating proved facts from hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause defined as an unconditionally invariable antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of a phenomenon is 'the antecedent, or the concurrence of antecedents, on which it is invariably and unconditionally consequent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate mere past regular succession with causation; to call an antecedent the cause we must believe that, given the present constitution of things, the antecedent will always be followed by the consequent (not merely that it always has been). Example/anti-pattern: day and night are invariable in experience but not unconditional, so night is not the cause of day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conditional vs unconditional sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: An invariable sequence is not causal unless the sequence is unconditional; sequences that depend on other antecedents are conditional and not causes in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a putative cause, ask whether the succession would persist under all changes of other circumstances. Use thought or actual 'experimentum crucis' to test whether a sequence is derivative (e.g., the sun's presence shows day would occur even without prior night).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include dispositions/states of preparation as conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a cause produces in an object a capacity or 'state of preparation' for producing some later effect, that capacity must be included among the conditions required for the later phenomenon—even though the capacity is not a substantive entity but a name for our assurance about future action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate not only immediately preceding facts but also prior causes that endowed objects with dispositions (e.g., paint on a wall giving it a property to appear white; gunpowder particles collocated for explosion). Avoid reifying dispositions as independent substances; treat them as contingent future facts expressed differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: List immediate antecedent conditions present just before the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions required for the occurrence of any phenomenon must (in the enumeration of conditions) be among the facts immediately preceding its commencement—i.e., the immediate antecedents that together make the phenomenon inevitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When specifying causes of a phenomenon, include the objects and properties present immediately before the event (e.g., presence of an explosive object is an immediately precedent condition of explosion), while recognizing some of those properties may themselves be effects of earlier causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal relation: cause need not strictly precede effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Although causes are often antecedent, a cause and its effect may be contemporaneous; the cause does not strictly have to precede the effect by a perceptible interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two phenomena are simultaneous, resolve which is cause by determining which preceded the other (if possible) or by which assemblage of phenomena invariably gives rise to the other. Do not assume simultaneity rules out causal interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conditions for production vs continuance of an effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions necessary for first production of a phenomenon may differ from those required for its continuance; some effects require the permanent presence of their producing agencies, others continue without the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating persistence, classify phenomena as instantaneous (requiring continual reproduction by the cause, e.g., illumination) or enduring (remaining until actively changed, e.g., a made plowshare). Consider negative conditions (absence of counteracting forces) in analyses of continuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause comprises two elements: a force and a collocation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the assemblage of conditions that constitutes the Cause of a phenomenon, distinguish (1) the presence of a force (a changing antecedent) and (2) the collocation or spatial/relational arrangement of objects required for the force to produce the particular phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state both elements when formulating causal explanations (e.g., bonfire requires fuel/collocation and the chemical action (force) between air and fuel). This prevents tautology and clarifies what must be present for production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only co-existences from the same cause can be unconditional laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-existences among effects of different causes cannot be universal laws in themselves; only co-existences between different and mutually independent effects of the same cause (i.e., different properties of the same agent) can claim to be independent, unconditional laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you observe regular co-occurrence of phenomena, investigate whether they share a common cause (same agent's properties). If they arise from different primeval causes, treat co-occurrence as contingent on the distribution of those causes rather than as a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept and limits of Permanent (primeval) causes
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist Permanent Causes (primeval natural agents) that have subsisted indefinitely (e.g., the sun, earth). Their original existence and distribution cannot be accounted for, and their distribution cannot be presumed uniform across space without direct evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace phenomena back through chains of antecedents to either properties of primeval causes or conjunctions of them. Do not assume universality of derived uniformities unless you can show the underlying primeval-cause distributions obey a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use decisive experiments to determine conditionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience itself teaches which sequences are conditional and which are unconditional; decisive or critical experiments (experimentum crucis) can reveal the true antecedents of a phenomenon (e.g., observing the sun's light directly shows it is the cause of day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experimental tests that isolate antecedents to settle whether observed regularities are fundamental or derivative. Relying solely on passive observation of sequence can mislead about causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate demonstrated facts from hypothetical extensions (e.g., Conservation of Force)
rubrics_metrics.description: When advancing broad theoretical claims (such as Conservation of Force), distinguish the part resting on proved facts (e.g., interchangeability and numerical equivalence among forms like heat and mechanical work) from the hypothetical parts (e.g., reduction of all forces to molecular motions or requirement of an ether).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit in peer-review or evaluation about which conclusions are empirically established and which depend on auxiliary hypotheses; avoid presenting speculative elements as settled law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define central terms precisely (force as potentiality of motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual clarity is essential: for example, 'force' is better defined as 'potentiality of motion' rather than strictly 'motion', because the ability to produce motion may exist without actual current motion (e.g., potential energy in lifted stone or coal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise definitions to avoid category errors (e.g., conflating potential and actual motion) when judging theoretical claims; check how authors define their key terms and whether those definitions are consistent with the phenomena discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture of laws yields conditional uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: From a limited number of unconditional sequences (causes), the co-existence of causes will produce many additional uniformities (conditional sequences) by intermixture of their laws; these uniformities are invariable only while the causes co-exist in the same manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring laws from observed regularities, analyze whether the regularity is a primary unconditional law or a derived law from the combination of more fundamental causes. Identify component causes to understand scope and limits of regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional definitional modification excluding negative conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If one confines the meaning of 'cause' to the assemblage of positive conditions without the negative, then instead of 'unconditionally' one should say 'subject to no other than negative conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether your causal definition includes negative conditions (absences) or only positive presences; choose the phrasing that best fits your methodological needs and state it when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain 'cause' as a useful generalization (avoid nominal rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejecting the word 'cause' (as some positivists do) forfeits a convenient generalization and a term that marks a fundamental distinction in science; causes that are themselves phenomena are ascertainable and useful for framing a rigorous Canon of Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discard causal terminology for fear of metaphysical implications; instead, use 'cause' to denote assemblages of antecedent phenomena that reliably give rise to consequents, and keep the term's use tied to observable, ascertainable relations.
